The product name. Upstream writes it in about 1,200 places: window titles, dialogs, error messages, agent prompts.
The product name inside links, where the space is encoded.
Installer and update file names, so a download is not called T3-Code-1.2.3.dmg.
The app ID (macOS bundle ID, Windows app user model ID). With upstream's ID the OS treats this app and T3 Code as the same app.
The Linux desktop entry and D-Bus names. With upstream's names this app overwrites T3 Code's launcher entry.
The development build's link scheme and profile folder, so `npm run dev` here and T3 Code's own dev build do not share a profile or steal each other's links.
The link scheme the OS routes to the app. With upstream's scheme, links meant for T3 Code open this app and the other way round.
The same link scheme, where code compares it against a URL's protocol.

Agents label the app's own tools with its name. The chat recognises those labels to show friendly tool names, so it has to accept the new name as well as the old.

The short form of the product name in running text, such as "T3 threads" or "T3's browser". It leaves alone T3 Connect, T3 Chat and T3 Tools, which are T3's own services and company, and bare "T3" used as data.
The data folder in the home directory (~/.t3). Sharing it with an installed T3 Code would mix two apps' databases, which may be on different versions.
